steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a security paper that measures upgradable smart contracts on Ethereum: why upgradability is needed, what security problems it brings, and what our study and detection tool contribute.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Smart contracts on Ethereum are immutable, but there are good reasons to upgrade them
- Upgradable smart contract (USC) patterns and libraries
- USCs are hard to get right: security vulnerabilities in practice
- Our measurement study: USC patterns and security risks
- Our tool USCDetector
- Results on Ethereum

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Smart contracts and immutability
  - building blocks of DApps: DeFi (cite), NFT (cite)
  - Sep 2023: more than 61 million smart contracts on Ethereum (cite), largest smart-contract blockchain
  - immutable design for transparency, trust decentralization: once deployed, no centralized entity can change/upgrade it
  - conflicts with legitimate reasons to upgrade: new features, patching vulnerabilities -> inconvenience
- USC patterns
  - since 2016, design patterns for USCs introduced on Ethereum (cite x4), widely adopted by DApps (cite x2)
  - third-party libraries, e.g. OpenZeppelin (cite), ease/accelerate USC development and deployment
- Security problems
  - developing USCs still challenging, developers need security awareness training (cite)
  - otherwise vulnerabilities -> attackers hijack USCs, affect users; not rare
  - widely adopted OpenZeppelin USC template: permanent state impairment, potential loss over $50m (cite)
  - attackers destroyed a USC and got all its ETH (cite)
  - more contracts with upgrade features -> more likely targeted in future (cite)
- Our study
  - large-scale measurement study of USCs and security implications in the wild
  - six commonly used USC patterns + implementations: straightforward (deploy new contract, migrate states), Ethereum built-in (Metamorphic contract), four methods splitting contract into two sub-contracts (one immutable, one modifiable)
  - series of security risks: off-path attackers destroy USCs (deny service), hijack contracts; users lose assets or trade deprecated tokens
  - first to systematically investigate several USC security issues at large scale
- USCDetector
  - previous work: source code analysis, limited USC types, e.g. proxy-based (cite)
  - ours: bytecode + transaction info (available for all contracts); detect six USC types, build upgrade chains, flag vulnerable ones
  - covers unverified (no source code) and verified contracts
  - evaluated on subset of verified contracts: 96.26% precision overall
- Results
  - 60,251,064 smart contracts; 10,218 upgrade chains; 91,959 USCs
  - proxy-based most popular; many developers mix approaches -> flexibility, batch processing
  - 15 USCs lacking restrictive checks on upgradable functions -> anyone can hijack
  - 118 vulnerable contracts that may completely disable USCs (unusable forever)
  - tokens of many deprecated contracts still listed on decentralized exchanges, affecting unaware users

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Smart contracts are important building blocks for decentralized applications (DApps), for example decentralized finance (DeFi) and NFT. As of Sep 2023, Ethereum, which is the largest blockchain that supports smart contracts, has more than 61 million smart contracts deployed on it. Ethereum and many other blockchains that support contracts use an immutable smart contract design, to enforce transparency and trust decentralization. This means that once a smart contract is deployed, no centralized entity can change or upgrade it. But immutability conflicts with many legitimate reasons for upgrading a deployed smart contract, like adding new features or patching security vulnerabilities, and this is inconvenient in practice. So since 2016 various design patterns for upgradable smart contracts (USCs) have been introduced on Ethereum, and DApps have widely adopted them. Many third-party libraries such as OpenZeppelin have also been developed to make USC development and deployment easier and faster.

Even with all these efforts, developing USCs is still hard and developers need to be trained with security awareness. If not, USCs might have security vulnerabilities that let attackers hijack the USCs and affect their users. Unfortunately such vulnerabilities are not rare in USCs. For example, an OpenZeppelin USC template that is widely adopted is vulnerable to permanent state impairment, which could cause huge financial loss (e.g., over $50m). Attackers have even managed to destroy a USC and get all its ETH. As more contracts integrate upgrade features, attackers are more likely to target these upgradeable contracts in the future.

- Our study
  - large-scale measurement study of USCs and security implications in the wild
  - six commonly used USC patterns + implementations: straightforward (deploy new contract, migrate states), Ethereum built-in (Metamorphic contract), four methods splitting contract into two sub-contracts (one immutable, one modifiable)
  - series of security risks: off-path attackers destroy USCs (deny service), hijack contracts; users lose assets or trade deprecated tokens
  - first to systematically investigate several USC security issues at large scale
- USCDetector
  - previous work: source code analysis, limited USC types, e.g. proxy-based (cite)
  - ours: bytecode + transaction info (available for all contracts); detect six USC types, build upgrade chains, flag vulnerable ones
  - covers unverified (no source code) and verified contracts
  - evaluated on subset of verified contracts: 96.26% precision overall
- Results
  - 60,251,064 smart contracts; 10,218 upgrade chains; 91,959 USCs
  - proxy-based most popular; many developers mix approaches -> flexibility, batch processing
  - 15 USCs lacking restrictive checks on upgradable functions -> anyone can hijack
  - 118 vulnerable contracts that may completely disable USCs (unusable forever)
  - tokens of many deprecated contracts still listed on decentralized exchanges, affecting unaware users

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Smart contracts are important building blocks for decentralized applications (DApps), for example decentralized finance (DeFi) and NFT. As of Sep 2023, Ethereum, which is the largest blockchain that supports smart contracts, has more than 61 million smart contracts deployed on it. Ethereum and many other blockchains that support contracts use an immutable smart contract design, to enforce transparency and trust decentralization. This means that once a smart contract is deployed, no centralized entity can change or upgrade it. But immutability conflicts with many legitimate reasons for upgrading a deployed smart contract, like adding new features or patching security vulnerabilities, and this is inconvenient in practice. So since 2016 various design patterns for upgradable smart contracts (USCs) have been introduced on Ethereum, and DApps have widely adopted them. Many third-party libraries such as OpenZeppelin have also been developed to make USC development and deployment easier and faster.

Even with all these efforts, developing USCs is still hard and developers need to be trained with security awareness. If not, USCs might have security vulnerabilities that let attackers hijack the USCs and affect their users. Unfortunately such vulnerabilities are not rare in USCs. For example, an OpenZeppelin USC template that is widely adopted is vulnerable to permanent state impairment, which could cause huge financial loss (e.g., over $50m). Attackers have even managed to destroy a USC and get all its ETH. As more contracts integrate upgrade features, attackers are more likely to target these upgradeable contracts in the future.

In this paper we do a large-scale measurement study to characterize USCs and their security implications in the wild. First we introduce six USC patterns that are commonly used and their implementations. Our work covers the straightforward method (e.g., deploying a new contract and migrating the states), the method built into Ethereum (i.e., Metamorphic contract), and four methods that split a contract into two sub-contracts (e.g., one immutable contract and one contract that can be modified). We also present a series of security risks that could have serious consequences. Some vulnerabilities might let off-path attackers completely destroy target USCs (e.g., deny their service) and even hijack existing contracts. Other issues might put users of smart contracts in danger, such as losing assets or trading deprecated tokens. As far as we know, we are the first to systematically investigate several USC security issues on a large scale.

We develop a tool called USCDetector to identify USCs and their security issues. Previous work relies on source code analysis and can only detect limited USC types (e.g., proxy-based). USCDetector is different, it collects various information like bytecode and transaction information, which is available for all contracts, to detect six types of USCs, construct their upgrade chains, and disclose ones that are potentially vulnerable. So USCDetector can cover both unverified (i.e., without source code) and verified smart contracts. We evaluate USCDetector on a subset of verified smart contracts and it achieves high accuracy, with 96.26% precision overall.

We use USCDetector on Ethereum, covering 60,251,064 smart contracts in total. USCDetecor constructs 10,218 upgrade chains and identifies 91,959 USCs. The results show some interesting observations: the proxy-based approach is the most popular one, but many developers try to mix different approaches to implement USCs, which gives more flexibility and helps batch processing. Also, USCDetector discloses multiple real-world USCs with potential security issues. For example, we found 15 USCs that lack restrictive checks on the upgradable functions, which could let anyone hijack them. We also found 118 vulnerable contracts that may completely disable USCs (e.g., they become unusable forever). We also found that tokens of many deprecated contracts are still listed in various decentralized exchanges, which affects many users who are not aware of it.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Smart contracts are critical building blocks for decentralized applications (DApps) such as decentralized finance (DeFi) [1] and NFT [2]. As of Sep 2023, more than 61 million smart contracts have been deployed on Ethereum [3], the largest blockchain supporting smart contracts. To enforce transparency and trust decentralization, Ethereum and many other contract-supporting blockchains adopt the immutable smart contract design, meaning that a smart contract, once deployed, cannot be changed or upgraded by any centralized entities. However, immutability conflicts with various legitimate reasons to upgrade a deployed smart contract, such as introducing new features or patching security vulnerabilities, which is inconvenient in practice. Thus, since 2016, various design patterns for upgradable smart contracts (USCs) have been introduced on Ethereum [4,5,6,7] and widely adopted by DApps [8,9]. Also, many third-party libraries, such as OpenZeppelin [10], have been developed to ease and accelerate USC development and deployment.

Despite these efforts, developing USCs is still challenging and requires developers to be trained with security awareness [11]. Otherwise, security vulnerabilities might exist in USCs that allow attackers to hijack them and further affect their users. Unfortunately, such vulnerabilities are not rare among USCs. For example, a widely adopted OpenZeppelin USC template is vulnerable to permanent state impairment that can potentially cause huge financial loss (e.g., over $50m) [12]. Attackers have even successfully destroyed a USC and obtained all its ETH [13]. With more contracts integrating upgrade features, attackers are more likely to target these upgradeable contracts in the future [14].

In this paper, we conduct a large-scale measurement study to characterize USCs and their security implications in the wild. We first introduce six commonly used USC patterns and their implementations. Specifically, our work covers the straightforward method (e.g., to deploy a new contract and migrate states), the Ethereum built-in method (i.e., Metamorphic contract), and four methods that decouple a contract into two sub-contracts (e.g., one immutable contract and one contract that can be modified). We also present a series of security risks that could potentially cause serious consequences. Some vulnerabilities might enable off-path attackers to completely destroy target USCs (e.g., deny their service) and even hijack existing contracts, while other issues might put smart contract users into dangerous situations, such as losing assets or trading deprecated tokens. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to systematically investigate several USC security issues on a large scale.

We develop a tool, USCDetector, to identify USCs and their security issues. Unlike previous work that relies on source code analysis [15] and can only detect limited USC types (e.g., proxy-based [15]), USCDetector collects various information such as bytecode and transaction information, which is available for all contracts, to detect six types of USCs, construct their upgrade chains, and disclose potentially vulnerable ones. Therefore, USCDetector can cover both unverified (i.e., without source code) and verified smart contracts. We evaluate USCDetector using a subset of verified smart contracts and show that it achieves high accuracy with an overall 96.26% precision.

We apply USCDetector on Ethereum, covering a total of 60,251,064 smart contracts. USCDetecor constructs 10,218 upgrade chains with 91,959 USCs identified. Our results show some interesting observations: while the proxy-based approach is the most popular one, many developers attempt to mix different approaches to implement USCs, which offers more flexibility and facilitates batch processing. Moreover, USCDetector successfully discloses multiple real-world USCs with potential security issues. For example, we identify 15 USCs lacking restrictive checks on the upgradable functions, potentially enabling anyone to hijack them. We also discover 118 vulnerable contracts that may completely disable USCs (e.g., make them unusable forever). Finally, tokens of many deprecated contracts are still listed in various decentralized exchanges, affecting many unaware users.
